274.title: Catherine of Siena
274.hook: a dyer's daughter who told popes what to do and nursed the plague-sick
274.carry: be who god meant you to be
274.howItsDone: Catholics honor Catherine as a saint and Doctor of the Church, with a feast day on April 29, and many Christians read her letters and her book, The Dialogue, as models of prayer that turns into bold action.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of a week, and Julian's great promise: all shall be well. Your line was all shall be well. Did you say it next to a worry? Day two hundred seventy-four.

Picture the most powerful person in your world. Now picture writing them a letter that begins warmly and then tells them, plainly, that they're doing it wrong and need to be braver. Most of us can't even send that email to a manager. In the 1370s, a young woman from Siena, in Italy, with no title, no money and no official role, wrote letters like that to the pope. And between letters, she was washing the bodies of plague victims. Today: Catherine of Siena.
screen: `THE MOST POWERFUL PERSON.` → `YOU'RE DOING IT WRONG.` → `WRITTEN TO THE POPE.`

segments.voice: Catherine Benincasa was born in 1347, the daughter of a wool dyer, one of the youngest of a very large family; tradition says more than twenty children. As a girl she decided to give her whole life to God, and her family pushed back hard, wanting her married. She refused. She didn't join a convent. She joined a group of lay women connected to the Dominican order, and lived at home, in a little room, praying. Then, in her twenties, she went out. She cared for the sick and the poor in Siena, and when plague came back, she nursed the dying and buried the dead. People gathered around her: friars, nobles, ordinary people, calling her mamma. And she started speaking up. At that time the popes lived not in Rome but in Avignon, in France. Catherine was convinced the pope belonged in Rome, and she told him so, in letter after letter, and even traveled to Avignon to say it in person. In 1377, the pope returned to Rome. Historians still debate how much she influenced that. She could barely write for much of her life; she dictated her letters, hundreds of them, to friends. There's a famous saying of hers on posters and mugs: be who God meant you to be and you will set the world on fire. Those exact words aren't hers. They're a loose modern version of a line in one of her letters, telling a friend that if he were what he ought to be, he'd set all Italy on fire. But the idea is truly hers. She died at thirty-three. In 1970 the Catholic Church named her a Doctor of the Church. Her boldness came from prayer, and it went out as love.
screen: `A DYER'S DAUGHTER.` · `THE PLAGUE-SICK OF SIENA.` · `LETTERS TO THE POPE.` · `SET ALL ITALY ON FIRE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you've been quiet about that you know you should say. To a friend, a boss, a family member, a group. Not a rant. One honest sentence, said with love. Picture saying it gently, the way Catherine began her letters, warmly, and then clearly. Notice the fear. Notice also what's underneath it: care. If you pray, you can ask for courage and kindness together. The bell holds the time.
Catherine of Siena. A dyer's daughter who nursed the dying and told popes the truth, with love.
Your line: be who god meant you to be. Today, speak up about one thing, gently. One sentence, with love. Day two hundred seventy-four.

275.title: The Imitation of Christ
275.hook: Thomas à Kempis's little book, read by Catholics and Protestants for five centuries
275.howItsDone: Many Christians, Catholic and Protestant above all, read The Imitation of Christ a few lines a day, often as part of morning or evening prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catherine of Siena, who nursed the dying and wrote to popes. Your line was be who God meant you to be. Did you speak up, gently? Day two hundred seventy-five.
screen: `BE WHO GOD MEANT YOU TO BE.`

segments.voice: Some books sit on a shelf and look important. Others get carried around until the spine cracks and the pages go soft. There's a small book, written in the Netherlands in the early 1400s, that has been that second kind for nearly six hundred years. Soldiers carried it. Prisoners read it in their cells. Catholic saints knew it almost by heart, and a founder of Methodism published his own edition of it. It has been translated into more languages than almost any book besides the Bible. And its author didn't even put his name on it. Today: The Imitation of Christ.
screen: `A SPINE CRACKED FROM USE.` → `SOLDIERS, PRISONERS, SAINTS.` → `NO NAME ON IT.`

segments.voice: The author was almost certainly Thomas à Kempis, a quiet monk who lived most of his long life in a small community near Zwolle, in what's now the Netherlands. He spent years copying manuscripts, including the whole Bible by hand, more than once. He belonged to a movement called the Modern Devotion, ordinary believers and religious communities who wanted a simple, heartfelt, practical faith. Not arguments. Life. The book opens with a line of Jesus from John's Gospel, in the King James Bible: "he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness." And then it asks, in effect: so, are you following? Not studying him. Following. It's full of short, sharp sentences. One says, roughly, that it's better to feel sorrow for your wrongs than to know how to define the word. Another says that on the day of judgment we won't be asked what we read, but how we lived. And one of its most famous lines is just two words in Latin: ama nesciri. Love to be unknown. Don't need to be seen. Do the good thing and let no one notice. Fittingly, Thomas never signed it. The book traveled for years without an author's name, and people argued over who wrote it. That's following quietly. Remarkably, it crossed every line the churches drew. Catholics treasure it. John Wesley, one of the founders of Methodism, put out his own English version. Many Protestants read it too, and so do some Orthodox Christians, though Orthodox writers have been more divided about it. Five centuries of Christians who disagreed about a great deal have agreed on this little book: the point is to walk the way he walked, quietly, every day.
screen: `A QUIET MONK NEAR ZWOLLE.` · `HE THAT FOLLOWETH ME.` · `AMA NESCIRI: LOVE TO BE UNKNOWN.` · `READ ACROSS EVERY CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line, or hear one. The Imitation is often read a sentence at a time. Take this one: love to be unknown. Settle, and breathe. Let it sit. Think of something good you did recently that you wanted someone to notice. Just notice the wanting, without judging it. Then imagine doing something good today that nobody will ever find out about. How does that feel? The bell holds the time.
The Imitation of Christ. A small unsigned book about following Jesus quietly, loved across the churches for five centuries.
Your line: follow quietly. Today, do one good thing no one will ever know about. Don't mention it. Not even later. Day two hundred seventy-five.

276.title: The interior castle
276.hook: Teresa pictures the soul as a castle of many rooms, God at the center
276.howItsDone: Many Christians, especially Catholics and Carmelites, read Teresa's Interior Castle as a guide to growing in prayer, and use her picture of rooms moving inward to describe the life of prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, The Imitation of Christ, and three Latin words: love to be unknown. Your line was follow quietly. Did you do something nobody saw? Day two hundred seventy-six.

Most of us live in the front hall of our own lives. We deal with the door: the messages, the noise, the people coming and going, the constant little emergencies. We rarely go further in. Some people go years without ever sitting quietly in the inner rooms of themselves. In 1577, a Spanish nun in her sixties, sick and overworked, was asked to write a book on prayer. She didn't know how to begin. Then, she said, a picture came to her. The soul is a castle. And most people never get past the outer wall. Today: the interior castle.
screen: `LIVING IN THE FRONT HALL.` → `A NUN WHO DIDN'T KNOW HOW TO BEGIN.` → `THE SOUL IS A CASTLE.`

segments.voice: Teresa of Ávila was a Carmelite nun in sixteenth-century Spain. She was funny, stubborn, practical and brave. She traveled rough roads by cart to found new convents, clashed with powerful people, and wrote some of the most loved books on prayer ever written. In The Interior Castle, she asks us to picture the soul as a castle made of a single diamond or very clear crystal, with many rooms, the way Jesus said there are many dwelling places in his Father's house. In the King James Bible: "In my Father's house are many mansions." Teresa's rooms are arranged in seven sets, like rings, one inside another. And at the very center, in the innermost room, lives God, the King, shining through the whole crystal. Here's the surprise. The castle is already yours. God is already at the center. You don't have to build anything. You have to go in. And the door into the castle, she says, is prayer. The outer rooms are noisy. Distractions crawl around like little reptiles, she says, snakes and lizards that come in with you from the courtyard. That's normal. You keep walking. Further in, prayer grows quieter and simpler, and more is given than done. In the innermost rooms, Teresa describes a union with God she compares to rain falling into a river: you can't tell the waters apart anymore. But she's firm about one thing. The test of how far in you've gone isn't feelings. It's love of your neighbor, and humility. In 1970 she and Catherine of Siena became the first women named Doctors of the Church.
screen: `A CASTLE OF CLEAR CRYSTAL.` · `GOD IN THE INNERMOST ROOM.` · `THE DOOR IS PRAYER.` · `THE TEST IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Picture a castle of clear crystal, light coming from its center. You're standing in a noisy outer room: your to-do list, your phone, today's worries crawling around. Don't chase them out. Just notice a door ahead of you. Walk through it, one room further in. It's a little quieter. Stay there. If you pray, you can simply turn toward the light at the center. The bell holds the time.
The interior castle. Teresa's picture of the soul: many rooms of clear crystal, with God living at the center.
Your line: there's a room further in. Today, when the front hall gets loud, take one breath and picture stepping through one more door. Day two hundred seventy-six.

what it means: God already lives at your center; prayer is the door, and the path goes room by room inward.

277.title: The dark night
277.hook: John of the Cross: sometimes God feels absent, and that's part of the road
277.howItsDone: Many Christians who go through long dry seasons in prayer find comfort in John of the Cross, and spiritual directors often use his idea of the dark night to help people keep praying when God feels far away.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the interior castle: rooms of crystal, God at the center. Your line was there's a room further in. Did you step through one more door? Day two hundred seventy-seven.

Many people who pray know this season, even if they've never said it out loud. Prayer used to feel warm. Church used to move you. God used to feel close. And then, sometimes for no clear reason, it goes quiet. The words feel empty. You sit down to pray and it's like talking into a closed room. You wonder if you're doing something wrong, or if it was all in your head. In the 1500s, a small Spanish friar, locked in a tiny prison cell by men of his own religious order, wrote about that exact experience. Today's word: dark night.
screen: `PRAYER USED TO FEEL WARM.` → `IT GOES QUIET.` → `A FRIAR IN A PRISON CELL.`

segments.voice: John of the Cross was a Carmelite friar, a close colleague of Teresa, whom we met yesterday. He worked with her to reform their order. Not everyone wanted reforming. In 1577 some of his own brothers seized him and locked him in a cell in Toledo so small and dark he had to stand on a stool to read by the light of a slit in the wall. He was beaten. He was there for months. And in that darkness he composed poetry. The best known begins: on a dark night. After months, the story goes, he escaped at night by a rope of strips torn from blankets. Later he wrote a long book explaining the poem, The Dark Night. Here's his idea. At the start, God often feels close and sweet, the way a mother carries a small child. But at some point, God sets the child down to walk. The warm feelings dry up. Prayer feels dark and empty. John says this is not God leaving. It's God working in secret, loving you past your feelings, so that you come to love God for God, not for how God makes you feel. You'll remember Bernard's four loves. John calls this darkness, strangely, a guiding night, a night more kindly than the dawn. The Psalms said it long before: "the darkness and the light are both alike to thee." One important note. John distinguished this spiritual dryness from other kinds of suffering, and many Christians today add: if the darkness includes deep sadness or hopelessness, talk to someone, a doctor, a counselor, a trusted friend. Both can be true. Dark is not absent.
screen: `A CELL IN TOLEDO, 1577.` · `ON A DARK NIGHT.` · `GOD SETS THE CHILD DOWN TO WALK.` · `DARK IS NOT ABSENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Gently remember a time when God, or meaning, or hope, felt far away. You don't have to relive it. Just hold it at arm's length. Notice: you got through it, or you're in it now. Either way, try saying quietly: dark is not absent. If you pray, you can simply sit in the dark with God, without needing to feel anything. The bell holds the time.
Dark night. John of the Cross's name for the season when God feels absent, and is still quietly at work.
Your line: dark is not absent. Today, if prayer or life feels flat, don't take it as the end of the road. It may be part of it. Day two hundred seventy-seven.

278.title: Brother Lawrence's kitchen
278.hook: a monastery cook found God as near among the pots as at the altar
278.howItsDone: Many Christians, Catholic and Protestant alike, read Brother Lawrence and try to turn to God briefly and often through the day, especially during chores and ordinary work.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was dark night, John of the Cross's season when God feels far. Your line was dark is not absent. Did it help on a flat day? Day two hundred seventy-eight.

Picture a busy kitchen at dinner time. Pots boiling over. Somebody shouting for more bread. Somebody else wants the salt. The floor is wet, the oven is too hot, and you have a limp and a bad back. Not exactly a holy place. In the 1600s, in a monastery in Paris, the cook was a clumsy former soldier who, by his own account, had a natural dislike of kitchen work. And yet visitors came away saying he was the most peaceful person they'd ever met. He said he felt God as near among the pots as in church. Today's word: practice of the presence.
screen: `POTS BOILING OVER.` → `A CLUMSY FORMER SOLDIER.` → `AS NEAR AS IN CHURCH.`

segments.voice: His name was Nicolas Herman. He grew up poor in France and became a soldier during a long and brutal war, and was wounded. The story he told later was that his faith first woke up at eighteen, looking at a bare tree in winter. He thought: soon it will have leaves again, and flowers, and fruit. And he felt, all at once, the goodness and care of God. Years later he joined the Carmelites in Paris as a lay brother, taking the name Brother Lawrence. They put him in the kitchen, where he worked for many years. Later, when his leg got worse, he repaired sandals. He never wrote a book. After he died, a friend gathered his few letters and the notes of their conversations into a little collection, The Practice of the Presence of God. Its idea is simple. Talk to God all day long, in ordinary moments, in your own plain words. Not only in set times of prayer, but while you work. When you wander off, which you will, just come back, without fuss. He said that the time of work was not different to him from the time of prayer, and that in the noise and clatter of the kitchen, with several people calling for different things at once, he felt God as calmly as if he were kneeling at the altar. He even said he turned his little omelet in the pan for the love of God. And when he'd finished, if there was nothing else to do, he'd pick up a straw from the floor for love of God. That's it. Nothing heroic. Just every small thing, done with God, in the room.
screen: `A BARE TREE IN WINTER.` · `A LAY BROTHER IN THE KITCHEN.` · `TALK TO GOD ALL DAY.` · `THE OMELET, FOR LOVE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wash dishes as prayer. If you're near a sink, you can do this for real. If not, picture it. The warm water, the soap, one plate at a time. With each dish, just be aware you're not alone. If you pray, you can say a word or two to God, plainly, the way you'd talk to someone standing beside you. If you don't, just give full attention to one plate. The bell holds the time.
Practice of the presence. Brother Lawrence's way: turning to God in every ordinary moment, even at the stove.
Your line: god among the pots. Today, pick one chore you don't like, and do it slowly, with God in the room. Day two hundred seventy-eight.

279.title: The inner light
279.hook: George Fox and the Quakers: there is that of God in everyone, found in silent waiting
279.howItsDone: Many Quakers gather for meeting for worship in silence, speaking only when they feel led; others, especially in Africa and the Americas, worship with pastors, hymns and sermons.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was practice of the presence: Brother Lawrence and his omelet. Your line was God among the pots. Which chore did you do with God in the room? Day two hundred seventy-nine.

Imagine walking into a plain room with wooden benches facing each other. No altar, no pulpit, no music. People come in and sit down. And then nothing happens. Nobody leads. Nobody speaks. Five minutes. Twenty. The only sounds are a cough, a creaking bench, a bird outside. And then, maybe, someone stands, says a few quiet sentences, and sits down again. Then more silence. For many Quakers, that is what worship looks like, and has for more than three hundred and fifty years. It began with a restless young man in England. Today: the inner light.

George Fox was born in 1624, in a time of civil war and religious turmoil in England. As a young man he was desperate for spiritual answers. He went from minister to minister, and none of them could help him. And then, he wrote in his Journal, when all his hopes in people were gone, he heard a voice that said, in his own old English: "There is one, even Christ Jesus, that can speak to thy condition." His heart, he says, leapt for joy. Fox came to believe that God speaks directly to every person, not only through clergy or buildings. He pointed to the Gospel of John, which says of Christ: "That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world." Every man, every person. Friends came to call this the inner light, or the light within. So Fox's followers, who called themselves Friends, and whom others nicknamed Quakers, would gather in silence and wait for that light to speak. In a letter from prison in 1656, Fox urged them to "walk cheerfully over the world, answering that of God in every one." That of God in every one. Not only in the people who agree with you. In the jailer. In the stranger. In the enemy. That conviction pushed many Friends into costly action over the centuries: early work against slavery, prison reform, refusing to fight in wars. Today there are different kinds of Quaker worship. Many meetings still wait in silence. Others, especially in Africa and the Americas, have pastors, hymns and sermons. But the conviction runs through all of them: there is something of God in everyone.
screen: `SPEAK TO THY CONDITION.` · `THE TRUE LIGHT, WHICH LIGHTETH EVERY MAN.` · `SILENT WAITING.` · `THAT OF GOD IN EVERY ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in silence, and if you can, with one other person. If someone is near, ask them to sit quietly with you for two minutes. No talking, no phones. If you're alone, picture someone you know sitting across from you. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to make anything happen. Just wait. If a thought feels like light, hold it. If it's only noise, let it pass. The bell holds the time.
The inner light. The Quaker conviction that God's light shines within every person, found by waiting in silence.
Your line: that of God in everyone. Today, with one person who annoys you, look for it. Just look. Day two hundred seventy-nine.

280.title: Seraphim of Sarov
280.hook: a Russian Orthodox hermit who greeted every visitor, my joy, Christ is risen
280.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians honor Seraphim as one of Russia's most beloved saints, and many greet each other with 'Christ is risen' through the Easter season, answering 'truly he is risen'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the inner light: George Fox and the silent meeting. Your line was that of God in everyone. Did you look for it in someone difficult? Day two hundred eighty, the end of the week.

Think about how you greet people. At the door, on the phone, at work. Hey. Hi. What's up. Usually it's automatic. Now imagine someone who greeted every single person who came to see him, rich or poor, sick or angry, a stranger or a sinner, the same way, every day of the year: bowing low, smiling, and saying, my joy, Christ is risen! Not just at Easter. In winter, in the middle of the week, to people he'd never met. That was an old monk in a forest in Russia, two hundred years ago. Today: Seraphim of Sarov.
screen: `HEY. HI. WHAT'S UP.` → `MY JOY, CHRIST IS RISEN!` → `EVERY DAY OF THE YEAR.`

segments.voice: Seraphim was born in the 1750s in the Russian town of Kursk and became a monk at the monastery of Sarov. After years in the community, he went to live alone in a small hut in the forest, praying, reading the Gospels, and working a little garden. Many stories are told about those years. People say he fed a wild bear from his hand. And tradition says that when robbers came, thinking he had money, he let them beat him nearly to death without resisting, and afterward asked that they not be punished. He recovered, bent over for the rest of his life. Then, after many years of silence, he opened his door. Crowds came. And every one of them heard the same greeting: my joy, Christ is risen! That's the Easter greeting of Orthodox Christians, when one person says Christ is risen and the other answers, truly he is risen. Seraphim said it all year round, as if every day were Easter and every visitor were his joy. He's remembered for a teaching that's often passed on in one line: acquire the spirit of peace, and thousands around you will be saved. The words vary in the telling, but the idea is clear. You can't argue or force people into peace. But a person who is truly at peace changes the room. People came to him anxious and left calm. In another famous conversation, he told a visitor that the true aim of the Christian life is to acquire the Holy Spirit. Not rules for their own sake. The Spirit, and peace with it. Look back at this week: Catherine's courage, the quiet Imitation, the castle, the dark night, the kitchen, the inner light, and now Seraphim. Each one, in a different way, was learning peace.
screen: `A HUT IN THE FOREST.` · `HE DID NOT RESIST.` · `EVERY DAY IS EASTER.` · `ACQUIRE THE SPIRIT OF PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of the next person you'll greet today. A family member, a coworker, the cashier. Picture them. Now picture greeting them as if they were a joy to you, just for a moment. Not fake. Just open. Notice what it does in you to see them that way. Let your own breathing slow. That's where peace starts. The bell holds the time.
Seraphim of Sarov. The Russian hermit who called everyone my joy, and taught that peace in one person spreads to many.
Your line: acquire peace. Today, greet someone warmly, more warmly than usual, as if they were a joy. Day two hundred eighty.

pairs: he asked they not be punished
the aim of the Christian life

myth: Seraphim said Christ is risen only at Easter
he greeted every visitor that way, all year round.
the peace saying has one fixed wording
the words vary in the telling; the idea is that peace in one person spreads.
Christ is risen is the Orthodox Easter greeting
one says Christ is risen; the other answers, truly he is risen.

fork.setup: robbers attack you in your forest hut, thinking you have money. you're strong enough to fight. what does tradition say Seraphim did?
options: he didn't resist, and later asked they not be punished.
he fought them off.
he ran to the monastery for help.
fork.reveal: he was beaten nearly to death, recovered bent over, and forgave them. peace, acquired the hard way.

original.note: Russian: my joy; Seraphim's greeting to every visitor.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hermit who hid from people.
what it means: a man who spent years in silence and came out able to greet everyone as a joy, and taught that peace spreads.
what a scholar hears: the Paschal greeting used all year; the conversation with Nicholas Motovilov on acquiring the Holy Spirit; and canonization in 1903.
